json.summary: A burly, foul-mouthed tradesman in a work vest parks his flatbed truck, locks it and walks off. A groan from the truck bed brings him back. Lying on the flatbed is a man he ran over on 'Gubacs Teréz út' a week ago last Tuesday. Both of the man's legs broke, and he has been lying there ever since, living off the two big bags of shopping he was carrying when he was hit. The driver swears, wanders off, and comes back not with an ambulance but with pillows and a blanket, because the nights are getting cold. The humour comes from how calmly both men treat an absurd hit-and-run, from the driver's coarse but oddly caring reaction, and from the ad on the truck, 'FELVESZEM' ('I pick up'), which turns out to be literally true.

characters.name: truck driver
characters.description: Heavy-set middle-aged tradesman with a big nose, slicked-back hair, stubble and a sleepy, grumpy look. He wears a multi-pocket work vest and owns the flatbed truck. He talks in coarse, working-class slang and swears in almost every line ('mi a faszom', 'mi a gecit', 'a kurva élet'). His verbal tic is 'bazme' (from 'baszd meg', roughly 'fuck it' or 'man'), which ends his sentences (r4, r8, r21). He clips his speech ('kamuzzá' instead of 'kamuzzál'). He reacts to the horror with irritation, then with gruff, misplaced care.

characters.name: injured man on the truck bed
characters.description: Never seen; only his voice comes from the covered flatbed. The driver hit him with the truck, and he has lain on the flatbed with both legs broken for about a week. He groans ('HRAHGHHRRR', 'AAAARRRGH'). He speaks in plain, calm, almost resigned sentences, with deadpan understatement ('fáj. fájogat.' – it hurts, it hurts on and off). He doesn't swear.

panels.description: The truck driver walks away from his parked flatbed truck, pointing his key fob at it. The hand-lettered 'HLOTT!' over the cab and 'RITY!' near the key look like sound effects of the door slamming and the lock chirping. A broom sticks up from the flatbed, and the side of the bed reads a garbled 'ÉPÖIPAI KITTELEZÉS • OG…', cut off at the edge.

Back view of the truck. A groaning bubble 'HRAHGHHRRR....' rises from the covered flatbed. The driver, hands on hips, says 'MI A FASZOM?' (tail to his mouth). The tailgate shows a phone number and 'FELVESZEM'.

The driver demands to know who is on his flatbed (tail to his mouth). A bubble whose tail leads into the flatbed gives the injured man's answer: he was hit on Gubacs Teréz út, both his legs broke, and he has been lying there since. The small 'FEKSZEM ITT.' (r6) is the last line of that answer, squeezed out at the edge of the bubble.
The driver leans on the truck and protests that he wasn't even near there today (tail to his mouth). The voice from the flatbed (tail goes down into the bed) says it happened a week ago last Tuesday.

The driver, waving a disbelieving fist, calls it a lie and asks how the man didn't starve (tail to his mouth). The voice from the bed, with a wavy tail into the flatbed, explains he was coming out of the shop when he got hit… with two big shopping bags.
The driver scratches his head, says 'A KURVA ÉLET!' and walks out of the frame to the right. The truck stands alone.
Only the truck is in view. Another groan 'AAAARRRGH....' rises from the flatbed.

The driver has come back and tosses pillows and a blanket onto the flatbed (motion lines), saying 'here's a blanket, nights are getting cold' (tail to his mouth). The bedding now piled on the truck bed is the punchline: he makes the victim comfortable instead of getting him help.

notes: Main joke: the driver ran someone over a week ago without noticing. The victim, with both legs broken, has been lying on the flatbed ever since. Neither man treats this as an emergency. The punchline (r21) is the driver's 'solution': instead of calling an ambulance or the police, he brings pillows and a blanket because 'the nights are getting cold'. Keep r21 casual and caring in a gruff way; the comedy is in how mismatched it is.

Tailgate sign 'FELVESZEM' (r3, r7, r11, r14, r16, r20, r22): a phone number plus 'felveszem', the usual hand-painted tradesman's ad meaning 'I'll pick up / I'll take it' (e.g. a call, a job, a load). 'Felvesz' also means 'to pick someone up' (a passenger) and 'to answer the phone'. Here it turns literal, because the man really did pick up a person. Translate it consistently as a short, ad-style phrase that can also mean picking up a person, e.g. 'WILL PICK UP' or 'PICKUPS TAKEN'. The number '7722.683' can stay as drawn. The sign is the same in every panel apart from small differences in hand-lettering ('7722·683', '7722 · 683'); these are not a scramble gag, so translate it the same way every time.

Truck side sign r0 'ÉPÖIPAI KITTELEZÉS • OG…': it reads as a garbled 'ÉPÍTŐIPARI KITTELEZÉS' ('construction-industry puttying/caulking'), cut off by the panel edge. It tells us the driver is a small-time construction tradesman with a homemade business sign. It is background flavour, not a punchline. Translate loosely (e.g. 'CONSTRUCTION CAULKING • …'); you can keep a slightly sloppy, misspelled look and keep it cut off.
'HLOTT!' and 'RITY!' in p0 are hand-drawn sound effects outside the boxes and can't be edited: most likely the door slamming and the lock chirping from the key fob. No translation needed.
r2 'MI A FASZOM?' – literally 'what my dick?'. A crude 'what the fuck?'. Strong swearing, but everyday for this character.

r4 'mi a gecit keresel a platómon' – literally 'what the cum are you looking for on my flatbed'. 'Geci' (cum) is a very vulgar intensifier; the line amounts to 'what the fuck are you doing on my truck'. 'Plató' = the open flatbed of a small truck.

Driver's verbal tic 'BAZME' (r4, r8, r21): a clipped form of 'baszd meg' ('fuck it', literally 'fuck it/him'), used as filler like 'man' or 'damn'. Use the same English filler every time, e.g. 'fuckin' hell' or 'for fuck's sake', so the tic stays visible. In r21 it softens into almost friendly filler, which is funny.
r15 'A KURVA ÉLET!' – literally 'the whore life!'. A standard Hungarian exasperated curse: 'fucking hell!' or 'for fuck's sake!'.

r12 'NE KAMUZZÁ!' – 'kamuzik' is slang for 'to lie, bullshit'. 'Kamuzzá' is a clipped form of 'kamuzzál' with the final -l dropped, which is typical of casual, working-class or rural speech. Something like 'Don't bullshit me!' or 'Quit yer bullshittin'!' fits.

r5 'A GUBACS TERÉZ ÚTON': a parody street name. It mixes Gubacsi út, a real busy road in Budapest's industrial south (District IX), with the pattern of streets named after people (e.g. 'Mária Terézia', or a 'Teréz' first name). 'Gubacs' also means 'oak gall', so it sounds slightly silly. Keep it as a Hungarian street name ('Gubacs Teréz út' or 'Gubacs Teréz Road'); no explanation needed.

r5 'FÁJ. FÁJOGAT.' – 'it hurts. It aches on and off.' 'Fájogat' is a frequentative/diminutive form ('keeps hurting a bit'). It is an absurd understatement for two broken legs left untreated for a week. Keep the flat, two-beat rhythm, e.g. 'Hurts. Kinda aches.'

r6 'FEKSZEM ITT.' ('so I'm lying here') ends the injured man's sentence in r5 ('…since then it hurts, it aches. I'm lying here.'). It is speech, not a sign, even though the detector marked it as one. Translate it as the end of r5.

r8 vs r9: the driver protests that he 'wasn't even near there today'. The victim calmly corrects him: it happened 'a week ago last Tuesday'. The driver's defence is about the wrong day, not about whether he hit someone.

r12–r13 garden-path joke: the driver asks how the man didn't starve in a week. The victim starts 'I was coming out of the shop when I got hit full on…' ('telibe kapott' = 'it got me square on'), then adds after a pause '…two big shopping bags'. In a quick read it sounds as if the bags hit him, but the real meaning is that he had two big bags of groceries with him, which is what he has been living on. Keep the ellipses and the delayed 'two big bags' so the reveal comes last. 'Szatyor' = shopping bag or carrier bag.
Groans r1 'HRAHGHHRRR....' and r19 'AAAARRRGH....' come from the injured man hidden on the flatbed (the bubble tails go down into the bed). Translate them as English pain groans of similar length.
Register contrast: the driver swears in almost every line; the victim speaks politely and plainly and never swears. Keep this contrast.
